urgent_first_check.interpretation: urgent_first correctly lets a later-arriving urgent order overtake an already-queued normal order at every stage; fifo correctly preserves arrival order. No bug found in PriorityStore usage.

state_leakage_check.interpretation: All 13 state features are derived from orders already arrived and currently queued/in-service, plus elapsed simulation time. The agent cannot see future arrivals, so any apparent urgent-prioritising behaviour is not genuine anticipation of future urgent demand. Separately, the state has NO worker-count / capacity feature at all — the agent cannot distinguish a low-capacity regime (e.g. s221) from a high-capacity one (e.g. s432); this is a distinct, confirmed generalisation weakness (§12), not a leakage issue.

reward_audit.interpretation: The reward rewards on-time urgent orders 7.0 reward-units more than a maximally-late urgent order, vs 5.0 for normal — a 1.4x imbalance favouring urgent completion. There is no terminal penalty for falling below the normal-SLA floor and no explicit starvation/age penalty. This creates a structural incentive to sacrifice normal orders whenever doing so improves urgent timeliness, with nothing in the reward pushing back once normal SLA collapses.

root_cause_interpretation: RL-3 normal-order starvation for December is NOT explained by a single consistent behaviour: on ['s432'] the agent picks urgent 100.0% of contested decisions (matching a 'reward favours urgent' story), while on ['s221'] it picks urgent only 25.6% of the time yet BOTH SLAs still collapse. That inconsistency rules out a simple 'reward always favours urgent' explanation as the sole cause. The more consistent explanation is RL generalisation failure (§12): the state has no capacity feature and its queue-length features are normalised by FIXED constants (/200 urgent, /500 normal, /5 WIP) that do not scale with regime capacity. Under heavy December load these features saturate at 1.0 (state_saturation_signal=True on the affected regime(s)), making the state uninformative and collapsing the learned policy to a fixed, regime-specific habit from training rather than a load-appropriate response. The underlying reward imbalance (see reward_audit) still matters — it shapes which fixed habit the agent falls into — but the regime-dependent flip in urgent-preference direction is the stronger, more specific evidence, and points at the state/generalisation design as the primary fix target (§12), not the reward alone.
changes_made: Added 3 normalised capacity features (picking/packing/dispatch worker count) to the RL-3 state vector (13 -> 16 dims), env_fullstage_rl.py::_state
Widened training regime sampling from 3 scenarios (s211 60%/s111 30%/s221 10%) to a uniform draw over the 12 stratified planning_profile.yaml::rl_generalisation.train_regimes
Rebalanced reward: w_normal 2.0->3.0, late_penalty_normal 1.0->2.0 (configs/rl3.yaml), narrowing the on-time<->late reward swing ratio between urgent and normal from 2.33x to 1.4x
Raised training episodes 60 -> 120 to preserve ~10 episodes/regime average under the wider regime mix
Retrained from scratch with all of the above combined into a single run; overwrote data/dqn_rl3_final.pt
honest_conclusion: The fix was principled and evidence-justified (the state generalisation gap and reward imbalance were both real, confirmed findings) but did NOT fully resolve the December anomaly on the two stress regimes re-tested after retraining. At s432 (an intentional holdout regime, never trained on) RL-3 still collapses to ~2% normal SLA at 100% urgent SLA, and its urgent-selection rate at contested decisions actually rose (97.4% -> 100.0%, streak 5303 -> 11137 consecutive urgent picks). At s221 (a trained regime) both SLAs still collapse (~1.7-1.8%) under December's genuinely extreme load for that capacity level -- the 12-regime generalisation evaluation shows FIFO and Urgent-First also collapse badly averaged across the 12 training regimes for December (mean_total_sla 0.014 and 0.32 respectively), because most of those regimes are simply undersized for December's 40,800-order peak. 120 episodes across 12 regimes (~10 episodes/regime) is likely too little training exposure per regime, especially for extreme-load months, to fully close this gap. Further training (more episodes, and/or a curriculum that oversamples high-load months) would likely be needed. This is reported as a confirmed partial improvement plus a remaining, honestly-flagged risk -- not a solved anomaly.
